video_title: Why PMs are suddenly valuable again | Tulsee Doshi (Head of Product, Gemini)
gist: Tulsee Doshi, head of product for Google's frontier models, says Google intends to win the frontier with Gemini 4 'Argon' while using its full stack (hardware to 14 billion-user products) and cost-quality Pareto coverage, and admits Google still lacks a strong personal-data assistant. She argues models are unpredictable, products should be built ahead of capability (60/20/20 rule), and PMs matter again because taste and coordination are scarce when building is cheap.

insights.claim: Google is positioning Gemini 4 (codename Argon) as its push to stay at the frontier, and its head of product rejects the idea that Google is not competing for the best-model title.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Google intends to compete head-on with frontier labs, not just on cost or distribution.
insights.quote: I actually think we do want to win the frontier conversation

insights.claim: The host states a widely held perception that Google lags the top two labs, Anthropic and OpenAI, having moments of leadership that then fade.
insights.speaker: Lenny (host)
insights.so_what: Market narrative of Google as #3 lab is a sentiment factor for GOOGL versus private labs.
insights.quote: A lot of people feel that Google lags behind the top two labs right now.

insights.claim: Google's AI strategy is full stack, running from its own hardware through models to end products, with roughly 14 products above a billion users (a stat she says she should double-check).
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Vertical integration plus distribution is Google's structural moat in AI.
insights.quote: I think the stat is like we have 14 products that are above a billion users.

insights.claim: Beyond frontier quality, Google aims to cover the whole Pareto curve of cost versus quality so different models serve search users, developers and cyber defenders.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Cost-efficient model tiers matter for margins at search scale and for winning price-sensitive API demand.

insights.claim: The host argues Google can win on multiple vectors at once: the most efficient cost-per-token frontier, the smartest model, and AI-enhanced existing products like AI Mode and AI Overviews.
insights.speaker: Lenny (host)
insights.so_what: Google's AI payoff may show up inside search/products even without chatbot leadership.

insights.claim: Google's frontier-model portfolio spans Gemini, gen-media models (video, image incl. Nano Banana, Lyria music), the Gemma open models, and audio models for dialogue, audio understanding, text-to-speech and translation.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Breadth across modalities gives Google multiple monetization surfaces beyond chat.

insights.claim: Doshi concedes Google has not yet shipped a compelling assistant built on users' Gmail, Calendar and Docs data, as third-party assistants increasingly harvest that data, but says the team is working on it.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: A Google-native personal-data agent is a pending catalyst; meanwhile startups capture value from Google's data.
insights.quote: I think you are right that like there is more work we need to do here on this front.

insights.claim: The host argues that like Apple, once Google ships a good personal assistant, its distribution advantage lets adoption ramp very quickly.
insights.speaker: Lenny (host)
insights.so_what: Late entry by Google into personal agents could still compress startups' window.
insights.quote: the distribution advantage is very strong and uh things can go really well really quickly

themes.theme: AI safety and the cyber defense opportunity

insights.claim: Google deploys monitors on models' chain of thought to detect misalignment and intervene, which she says increases confidence in deployment and helps improve models.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Chain-of-thought monitoring is becoming a standard deployment control for frontier labs.

insights.claim: With Gemini 4, Google is actively partnering with cyber defenders including Wiz, now a Google company, whose Scan for Good program found and patched a vulnerability at a hospital system.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: AI-powered vulnerability discovery is a concrete revenue and positioning angle for Google Cloud security.
insights.quote: partnering with whiz that is now a Google company

insights.claim: The host relays an All-In discussion that as AI gets very good at cyber offense, organizations will spend much more on AI-driven cyber defense.
insights.speaker: Lenny (host)
insights.so_what: Supports a secular spending increase for AI-enabled cybersecurity vendors.
insights.quote: people are going to be investing a lot more in cyber defense and AI for protecting

insights.claim: Doshi frames safety optimism as conditional: the path to optimism runs through people actively worrying about and interrogating how models are built.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Signals Google's safety posture is process-driven rather than declaring the problem solved.
insights.quote: the path to optimism is through thinking about it

insights.claim: Model outcomes are not fully predictable even with goals and evals set; the PM's job includes discovering where a trained model unexpectedly shines and turning that into products.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Capability roadmaps from labs carry inherent uncertainty; surprises in either direction are normal.
insights.quote: The model isn't predictable. It's kind of like Snape's potions class.

insights.claim: Model behavior and persona are treated as the model's UX: Google's model-behavior team builds a spec of what good looks like for Gemini, translates it into rubrics, eval data and reward modeling.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Personality/behavior is a deliberate differentiator in commoditizing model markets.

insights.claim: The host relays from a frontier-lab PM that labs intentionally ship frontier capability fast, even with messy UX, to stay competitive and learn what users do with it.
insights.speaker: Lenny (host)
insights.so_what: Competitive pressure favors speed over polish, creating openings for UX-focused application layers.
insights.quote: there's this kind of urgency to get frontier power of AI out to users as fast as possible

insights.claim: UX latitude depends on the audience: AI Mode for billions of search users needs accessible UX, while Antigravity targets power users comfortable with slash commands, terminals and IDEs.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Google segments AI surfaces by user sophistication, supporting both mass-market and developer tooling bets.

insights.claim: Accurate evaluation must be end to end: judge-model quality, production mitigations and filters, and serving setup all affect measured performance, especially for audio naturalness.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Benchmark claims may not reflect real-world served performance; evaluate vendors on full stack.

themes.theme: Building ahead of the models: the 60/20/20 rule

insights.claim: Under her 60/20/20 rule, builders should ship products where about 60% works now, 20% works well enough with near-term model gains in view, and 20% is aspirational where only glimmers of capability exist.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Startups that build ahead of model capability capture upside as models improve; rigid MVPs get stranded.
insights.quote: build such that like 60% of what you've built works now

insights.claim: Even someone who works on the model finds it hard to say where models will be in three months, so builders should use their own product-level proxies instead of betting on a lab roadmap.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Lab insiders admit limited forecastability; discount precise capability timelines.

insights.claim: Customers that built rigid systems around older model limitations get hampered when models improve, so products must stay adaptive and consistently retest.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Heavy scaffolding/wrapper businesses face obsolescence risk as base models improve.

insights.claim: The host relays the common view that 'the model is going to eat your harness for breakfast', citing Boris Churnney (as transcribed)'s advice to periodically remove skills and see if the model does as well on its own.
insights.speaker: Lenny (host)
insights.so_what: Value of harness/tooling layers may erode as models absorb their functions.
insights.quote: the model's going to eat your harness for breakfast

insights.claim: A harness is the wrapper around the model: system instructions, tools, skills and context that give the model an environment to operate in.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Clarifies where application-layer differentiation lives relative to base models.

insights.claim: After a phase of 'we don't need PMs', PMs are becoming valuable again because when anyone can build, people build things nobody wants, and deciding what is worth building is scarce.
insights.speaker: Lenny (host)
insights.so_what: Taste and product judgment become the bottleneck as AI commoditizes building.
insights.quote: people are realizing there's a very specific skill to figure out what is worth building

insights.claim: When anything can be built easily, building something great becomes the unique value add, making taste and the ability to turn chaos into order more important, since speed can otherwise introduce chaos.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Organizational coordination, not engineering capacity, becomes the constraint in AI-era product orgs.
insights.quote: building something great actually is now a a unique value ad

insights.claim: Google DeepMind increasingly hires PMs who play with models daily, have opinions on model 'vibes', can dig into data and build evals, and who rewrite roadmaps constantly as the space changes every two weeks.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Shows how frontier labs reorganize talent; roadmap half-lives are now weeks.
insights.quote: I think the space is changing every two weeks.

insights.claim: Start evals small: even five to 20 prompts that separate model A from model B, with yourself as rater, already give strong signal before scaling up.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Lightweight evals lower the bar for enterprises to compare model vendors and switch.
insights.quote: start with even just five prompts

insights.claim: Google replaced the six-tone Fitzpatrick scale, built for healthcare and skewed light, with Harvard professor Monk's 10-tone scale in its evaluations, improving products like the Pixel camera and image generation.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Eval design choices directly shape product quality and representation.

insights.claim: AI has shifted the PM from writing requirements for others to bringing 'heft' themselves through prototypes, evals or data, reflected in the 'X is the new PRD' trend.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: PM tooling (prototyping, analytics, evals) is a growing software category.

insights.claim: In docs, the model should provide the data and humans the insight; AI is ideal for post-launch usage roundups pulling dashboards, Twitter and Reddit feedback.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Defines where AI writing tools add value versus generating 'AI slop'.
insights.quote: what you should be providing is the insight. What the model should be providing is the data.

insights.claim: Her team shares reusable technical skills built on internal tools like Jet Ski, creating an iteration flywheel, and is running a two-day November workshop pulling all PMs off their day jobs to build with tools.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Large incumbents are investing in internal AI upskilling, accelerating enterprise agent adoption.

insights.claim: Burnout comes less from hours than from churn/chaos and unenjoyable grunt work, so AI tools that remove grunt work could reduce burnout even as everyone on her team works all the hours.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Productivity gains are being reinvested in more output, not fewer hours, amid fierce competition.
insights.quote: I think every single person on the team right now is putting in all of the hours

insights.claim: The host's survey of tech workers found more hours does not equal burnout; many are working their hardest yet having the best time of their careers.
insights.speaker: Lenny (host)
insights.so_what: AI-era intensity is sustainable for motivated talent, supporting continued high output at labs.
insights.quote: more hours does not equal burnout

insights.claim: Her Stanford flash-teams research with Michael Bernstein on assembling crowdsourced workers via MTurk maps onto today's design of efficient multi-agent sub-agent systems.
insights.speaker: Tulsee Doshi
insights.so_what: Human-workflow coordination research is being reapplied to agent orchestration.
